subject: chemistry
title: Practical: pH change during neutralisation
key_idea: You can follow neutralisation by measuring pH as a base is added to an acid. The pH starts low, rises as hydrogen ions react with hydroxide ions, and ends above 7 when the base is in excess.

blocks.text: The pH scale runs from 0 to 14 and measures how acidic or alkaline a solution is. This section covers how to measure it.

items.meaning: A scale from 0 to 14 that measures acidity or alkalinity.
A mixture of dyes that gives a range of colours across the pH scale.
An electronic probe that gives the pH as a number.

items: With universal indicator solution or paper, match the colour to a colour chart to find the approximate pH.
With a pH probe, wash the probe with water, put it in the solution and read the number.
Litmus only shows whether a solution is acidic or alkaline. It does not give the pH.

diagram.alt: Sort pH values and indicator colours into acidic, neutral and alkaline.
diagram.prompt: Sort each reading into the right group

items: Acids have pH below 7, neutral is 7 and alkalis are above 7.
Universal indicator and a colour chart give an approximate pH. A pH probe gives a number.

sections.heading: The practical: adding a base to an acid

blocks.text: This practical records how the pH of dilute hydrochloric acid changes as powdered calcium hydroxide or calcium oxide is added.

items.text: Use a measuring cylinder to put a fixed volume of dilute hydrochloric acid into a beaker.
Place a drop on universal indicator paper with a glass rod, or use a pH probe.
Add a measured portion of the powder, for example 0.1 g, and stir.
Use a new piece of indicator paper each time.
Keep adding portions and measuring the pH until it stops changing.

items: Stir after each addition. This mixes the substances evenly and makes them react and dissolve.
Measure the mass of the base on a balance, rather than using a spatula measure each time.
A pH probe gives the pH as a number and does not need a colour chart.

diagram.alt: A sketch (shape only, not real data) of a curve showing pH rising from low to above 7 as portions of base are added, then levelling off.

items: Add the base in measured portions and stir. Measure the pH after each one.
Stop when the pH stops changing.

blocks.text: The pH changes because hydrogen ions are used up. Explain it in three parts: start, reaction and end.

items: **Start:** the solution is acidic. It has a high concentration of H⁺ ions, so the pH is low.
**Reaction:** the base (hydroxide ions) reacts with the acid. This is neutralisation.
**End:** the concentration of H⁺ ions has fallen and there are excess OH⁻ ions, so the pH is above 7.
Adding acid to an alkali works the other way round. A strong alkali such as sodium hydroxide starts at about pH 12 to 14.
The pH falls as acid is added. With excess acid it ends at about pH 0 to 3.
Hydrogen ions react with hydroxide ions, so the H⁺ concentration falls and the pH rises.
With excess base, OH⁻ ions are left over and the pH is above 7.

checks.q: Describe how to measure the pH of a solution when a pH meter is not available.
checks.a: Add universal indicator solution (or use pH paper), note the colour produced and match it to a colour chart to find the pH.

checks.q: Why is the mixture stirred after adding each portion of powdered base?
checks.a: To mix the substances evenly, so the base reacts and dissolves and the reaction is complete.

checks.q: Explain, in terms of ions, why the pH of dilute hydrochloric acid rises when calcium hydroxide powder is added.
checks.a: The hydrogen ions react with the hydroxide ions (H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O). The concentration of H⁺ ions falls, and with excess hydroxide ions the pH is above 7.

worked_example.question:
Sulfuric acid and sodium hydroxide react to produce sodium sulfate.

Sulfuric acid is gradually added to sodium hydroxide solution.

The pH of the mixture changes as the sulfuric acid is added until in excess.

Suggest the pH at:
• the start before sulfuric acid is added
• the end when sulfuric acid is in excess.
answer_points: At the start: a value in the range 12–14.
At the end: a value in the range 0–3.
worked_example.tip: Give the start value first, then the end value. The start is the high value and the end is the low value.

worked_example.question:
In an experiment, powdered calcium hydroxide was added to dilute hydrochloric acid and the pH was measured.

The method used was

step 1 measure 200 cm3 dilute hydrochloric acid into a beaker
step 2 add 0.1 g of powdered calcium hydroxide to the beaker
step 3 find the pH of the mixture
step 4 repeat steps 2 and 3 until the pH stops changing.

Explain why the pH starts at a low value and ends at a higher value.
answer_points: Start: the solution is acidic, with a high concentration of H⁺ ions, so the pH is low.
Reaction: neutralisation. The hydroxide (alkali) reacts with the acid, H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O.
End: the concentration of H⁺ ions has reduced and there are excess OH⁻ ions, so the pH is above 7.
worked_example.tip: One mark each for start, reaction and end. Describing the pattern of the pH scores nothing.

worked_example.question:
Magnesium burns in oxygen to make magnesium oxide.

Magnesium oxide reacts with water to make an alkaline solution.
Describe how you would measure the pH of the magnesium hydroxide solution.
A pH meter is not available.
answer_points: Add universal indicator solution (or use pH paper).
Match the colour to a colour chart to determine the pH.
worked_example.tip: Because a pH meter is not available, the answer must use universal indicator or pH paper.
